claim: The low likelihood of detaching at low windspeeds when dry (due to higher average wind speeds) and when wet (due to pappus closure) means that dispersal largely occurs when wind speeds are high.

evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the modeling results shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effect on long-distance dispersal is particularly significant as this has a disproportionate effect on ecological distributions and is often the major driver of range expansion.
source: The effect on long-distance dispersal is particularly significant as this has a disproportionate effect on ecological distributions and is often the major driver of range expansion (Clark, 1998; Kot et al., 1996; Trakhtenbrot et al., 2005).

claim: Pappus morphing may have additional functions beyond detachment, flight, and dispersal, such as protection from damage, or to aid germination.
source: Pappus morphing may have additional functions beyond detachment, flight, and dispersal, such as protection from damage, or to aid germination.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about other possible functions.

claim: The morphing phenomenon occurs in many (perhaps most) pappus-bearing diaspores but is conspicuously missing from some representatives of the Asteraceae (e.g. Leontodon, Hieracium, Erigeron).
source: The morphing phenomenon occurs in many (perhaps most) pappus-bearing diaspores but is conspicuously missing from some representatives of the Asteraceae (e.g. Leontodon, Hieracium, Erigeron) (Rothert, 1895; Taliev, 1894).

claim: A comparative approach examining the ecological and phenological features of pappose fruits that do or do not morph may yield greater insight into the roles of pappus morphing.
source: A comparative approach examining the ecological and phenological features of pappose fruits that do or do not morph may yield greater insight into the roles of pappus morphing.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion for future research.

claim: Understanding of structural functions within environmental contexts is critical to predict the ecological consequences of climate change.
source: Considering how prevalent environmentally induced plasticity is in plant structure and its development, understanding of structural functions within environmental contexts is critical to predict the ecological consequences of climate change (Denny and Helmuth, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the broader significance of the research.

claim: Insights into ecological and environmental drivers enable us to comprehend selective pressure that has acted and will act to evolve plant forms and their functions.

claim: The mean increase in weight after wetting was 70 µg, which corresponds to approximately 10% greater weight when wet compared to dry.

claim: The turbulent intensities used in the detachment experiments are comparable to that in some natural conditions.

claim: Turbulence in the atmospheric boundary layer exhibits enormous variability, with values as high as 400% reported.

claim: Field-measured RH > 90% is a good proxy for wetness on plant surfaces.
source: As dandelion pappi can partially close at RH > 70% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) and field-measured RH > 90% is a good proxy for wetness on plant surfaces (Sentelhas et al., 2008), we used RH = 90% as a cut-off point.
evidence: This is cited to justify the choice of RH threshold in the modeling.

claim: Diaspore falling velocities for dry and wet conditions were 0.3 m s–1 and 0.7 m s–1, respectively, corresponding to the measured values from drop tests.
